draft.title: Headline and underlying inflation
card: the change in the whole consumer price index (CPI) over a period, usually a year. It counts every item in the CPI basket, including items with big price swings.
a measure that removes the biggest price swings to show the trend. The trimmed mean is one example.
The trimmed mean sorts all the price changes in the CPI from smallest to largest. It then leaves out the biggest rises and the biggest falls and averages the rest.
A one-off jump in the price of a single item, such as fuel or fruit after a flood, can lift headline inflation. Underlying inflation moves much less, so it gives a better guide to the ongoing trend.
draft.remember: Headline counts every price change. Underlying trims the extremes to show the trend.

a.q: What does the trimmed mean do to the price changes in the CPI?
opts: Drops the largest rises and falls, then averages the rest
Adds the largest rises and falls to the average
Counts only the items whose prices have fallen
Counts only the items that households buy most often
a.why: The trimmed mean removes the extreme price changes at both ends and averages what is left, so it shows the trend. Counting every item is what headline inflation does, so it is not the trimmed mean.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the biggest swings at each end.

b.q: A drought lifts vegetable prices sharply in one year. Headline inflation is 4.2% and the trimmed mean is 3.1%. What is the best reading of these figures?
opts: The one-off jump explains the gap, so the trend is near 3.1%
The trend is 4.2%, because headline counts every price rise
The trimmed mean is wrong, because it skips the vegetables
Both figures show the same trend, as both use one basket
b.why: The drought pushed up headline inflation, but the trimmed mean cuts out the biggest swings, so it is a better guide to the trend. Headline inflation is not wrong, but it mixes the trend with one-off price jumps.
b.clue: Which measure is built to filter out a sudden jump in one group of prices?

a.best: Drops the largest rises and falls, then averages the rest

b.best: The one-off jump explains the gap, so the trend is near 3.1%
